confounds: The diagnosed/control classes are highly imbalanced: 618 diagnosed versus 5,463 controls; rare-event estimates are noisy.
Diagnosed users have longer retained timelines on average, making user prevalence and per-timeline rates essential.
Fandom, queer-identity, pronoun, and entertainment signals may primarily reflect age, gender, sexuality, platform subculture, or sampling composition.
Self-disclosure of treatment or diagnosis may be related to annotation or recruitment pathways rather than latent depression itself.
Portuguese slang, spelling variation, replies, quotations, lyrics, memes, advocacy, news, and third-person discussion create substantial semantic-role ambiguity.
Politics, sports, COVID, and other event-driven topics may reflect collection windows, prolific retweeting, or temporal shocks.
Access to psychotherapy, psychiatry, medication, school, and work varies with socioeconomic status and demographic composition.
Lexical heuristics for first-person experience are imperfect and should not be treated as clinical classifiers.

caveats: Treatment access and self-disclosure may reflect collection or socioeconomic differences rather than symptom severity.
Medication and consultation words are ambiguous unless paired with possessive or first-person action cues.
findings.evidence_summary: Personal framing sharply improved the signal: care references occurred in 49.8% of diagnosed users versus 20.9% of controls, with higher normalized post frequency and consistent fold direction.
findings.prompt_guidance: Upweight persistent self-reports involving one's therapist, psychiatrist, treatment, or medication; downweight generic advice, physical-health medication, quotations, and discussion of someone else.

quantitative_support.measure: users with at least one first-person, non-obviously quoted mental-health-care post

findings.signal: First-person psychotherapy, psychiatric-care, or psychotropic-medication narratives.

caveats: A diagnostic word may refer to another person, a disease such as COVID, advocacy, stigma discussion, or a joke.
This is observable self-disclosure, not independent confirmation of diagnosis.
findings.evidence_summary: Self-framed diagnostic language was about twice as prevalent among diagnosed users; unqualified mentions of depression were substantially noisier than personal formulations.
findings.prompt_guidance: Treat self-attribution, personal diagnosis, laudo, or disorder descriptions as stronger than generic mentions; require first-person context and corroboration across posts.
findings.signal: Explicit self-labeling or diagnostic language, including depression or disorder terms, when clearly about the user.

caveats: The self/other and quote filter is heuristic and cannot fully remove lyrics, memes, or temporary situational complaints.
Isolation can coexist with substantial online friendship, fandom, and relationship discussion.
findings.evidence_summary: Self-framed distress and isolation were both more common and more repeated among diagnosed users. However, active relationship and social-participation language remained common in both groups.
findings.prompt_guidance: Prefer repeated, self-experienced distress plus isolation patterns over isolated negative words; do not require complete social inactivity.

quantitative_support.measure: users with at least two self-framed isolation/withdrawal posts

findings.signal: Persistent first-person distress combined with loneliness, withdrawal, or being socially cut off.

caveats: Lyrics, dark humor, advocacy, quotations, and discussion of someone else remain plausible false positives.
This corpus signal is not a clinical or safety assessment.
findings.evidence_summary: Strong self-framed risk expressions were uncommon but over twice as prevalent in diagnosed users, with the same direction in every development fold.
findings.prompt_guidance: Use only as a high-salience, low-recall feature when self-reference and contextual persistence are present; never infer imminent risk from a keyword alone.

quantitative_support.measure: users with first-person self-harm or severe death-ideation expressions

findings.signal: Rare first-person self-harm, suicide, or not-wanting-to-live language.

caveats: Some markers may reflect ordinary deadlines, illness, or educational circumstances.
Posting and age differences may affect the opportunity to mention school or employment.
findings.evidence_summary: Narrow impairment markers separated labels consistently, while broad work/study vocabulary was nearly universal and uninformative.
findings.prompt_guidance: Look for first-person inability, absence, dropout, procrastination, or loss of motivation tied to work or study; ignore ordinary work, class, or exam discussion alone.

quantitative_support.measure: users with explicit self-framed work/study impairment markers
users mentioning work or study topics in any context

findings.signal: Specific personal difficulty attending, completing, or sustaining work or study, rather than generic topic mentions.

caveats: Future language is context-sensitive and may concern short-lived events, finances, relationships, or jokes.
The simultaneous presence of positive plans is common and should be treated as counterevidence against a simplistic binary interpretation.
findings.evidence_summary: Negative-future language was more prevalent and more persistent in diagnosed users, but positive future and planning language was not absent from their timelines.
findings.prompt_guidance: Model negative future statements as one component of a broader pattern; do not equate ordinary uncertainty or delayed plans with hopelessness.

quantitative_support.measure: users with first-person negative-future or hopelessness language
users with at least two negative-future posts

findings.signal: Self-framed hopelessness, lack of plans, or expectations that circumstances will not improve.

caveats: The broad lexical category includes common non-psychiatric complaints and demographic topics.
No claim of clinical specificity or causal relation is supported.
findings.evidence_summary: Self-framed physical-symptom language was modestly higher among diagnosed users in every fold, but the category had high prevalence and broad coverage.
findings.prompt_guidance: Use physical symptoms only as supportive evidence when persistent and linked to personal distress or impairment; do not use isolated fever, menstrual, diet, or routine illness mentions.

quantitative_support.measure: users with first-person physical, sleep, energy, or pain complaints

findings.signal: Repeated self-reported bodily discomfort, sleep/energy problems, or somatic complaints.

caveats: This pattern is highly vulnerable to age, gender, sexuality, platform-community, and sampling confounds.
Entertainment and identity terms can occur in quotations, news, lyrics, or discussion of others.
findings.evidence_summary: Fandom and queer/gender identity terms were consistently more common and more intensive in diagnosed timelines, representing a useful contextual signal beyond symptom words.
findings.prompt_guidance: Use these topics as cohort/context variables or interactions with self-experienced distress, not as standalone clinical evidence; distinguish self-identity from advocacy or third-person discussion.

quantitative_support.measure: queer, gender, or pronoun identity vocabulary

findings.signal: Higher engagement with fandom/entertainment communities and identity-related vocabulary.

caveats: This may reflect collection period, political events, retweeting habits, age, or demographic composition.
Topic presence alone is weak; the distinction is mainly intensity after separating users from raw posts.
findings.evidence_summary: User presence was similar, but controls produced substantially more politics/news posts per user and per timeline post, with the intensity direction stable across folds.
findings.prompt_guidance: Treat repeated public-affairs/news engagement as a control-leaning activity or collection-context feature, not as evidence of better mental health.
findings.signal: Higher-intensity public-current-events, politics, and news discussion in controls.

caveats: The fold inconsistency indicates limited robustness.
Football-club and event-specific collection effects may dominate this signal.
findings.evidence_summary: Sports topic prevalence was identical by user, while controls generally posted more sports content; the direction weakened and slightly reversed in one fold.
findings.prompt_guidance: Use sports intensity only as a weak contextual feature and combine it with other evidence; do not interpret sports absence as a symptom.
findings.signal: Control-leaning sports discussion intensity, with weak user-level separation.

negative_results: Positive future/planning vocabulary was not reduced: at least one positive-future cue appeared for 99.8% of diagnosed users versus 99.0% of controls.
Generic work/study, relationship, and social-participation topics were near-universal; simple absence of these topics is unsupported.
Humor markers had very high prevalence in both groups and an unstable intensity difference, so laughter tokens alone are weak evidence.
Sports topic presence was virtually identical by user; only posting intensity leaned controlward, with one fold reversing slightly.
Diagnosed users had longer timelines on average (about 627 versus 530 posts), so raw topic counts without user-level prevalence or timeline normalization are misleading.
